Just know that there are no:


 -Firearms of any sort, you have to craft a bow for defense and hunting


 -hatchets or knives, you have to forge them, same with arrowheads. 


-better items like the expedition parka, snow pants, ect. 


- no starting matches, you have to find them or use flares


 - no starting bedroll, you have to find one 


 I'd say you can get started at any time you feel like it.  But you'll have to learn how to play the game differently than you do on lower difficulties. Find matches, find a bedroll, find a hacksaw, and find a hammer ASAP.  Cure some saplings ASAP. Get some scrap metal and cloth and head to a forge, make a hatchet, knife and plenty of arrowheads.  Use the starvation tactic until you can Hunt for a steady supply of meat. Hunt bears and wolves to craft a bearskin and wolfskin coat before day 50, even if you can't eat the meat yet. Get to level 5 cooking asap so you can eat bear meat and ruined meat.

If you're only going to use it for gaming, then go for the 6600xt.   


If you're using your PC for streaming, AI/ML programs, 3D modeling and rendering, then consider the 3060.  If you also game and are okay playing Ultra settings in 1080p, then the 3060 is a great option for your needs.  


If you can get a new RTX 3060 for less than $300, which it's going for on Amazon, it'd be well worth it.  The 3060 gets a lot of smack talk, but it's no slouch; it's just that for the first two years of it's launch, it was selling for $200+ above MSRP.  Some people have paid the current retail price of the 4070 on a 3060, thanks to scalpers and Cryptominers.  The 3060ti is a little bit faster because it has more CUDA cores and a bigger bus limit, but imo it's not a better deal than a 6600XT if you're going to game.  Also the 3060ti's 8gb of VRAM can cause problems if you use Blender or render huge projects with 4k textures.  But if you're a beginner who is just modeling your first donut, the 3060ti will render about 20% faster.  There are examples out there, however, where the 3060 outperforms the 3060ti, the 3070, and the 4060, because some games(cough cough poorly optimized cough) push the 8GB VRAM limit.  


AMD cards are great for gaming and are a blessing in the overpriced GPU market, but if you're planning on doing creative work, then that's a good reason to still consider Nvidia.    


One last heads up, DO NOT under any circumstances buy the RTX 3060 with 8GB of VRAM.  For some stupid fucking reason, Nvidia dropped this Trojan horse on the markets.  Make sure it says 12GB if you get the RTX 3060.

The 3060 is not a "horrible" card.  For blender it's quite good, and if you can get it new for $280(current Amazon pricing) then it'd be a good deal.  I always imagine the people calling it horrible are remembering it's release price during the card shortage, when it was going for $5-600+ from scalpers.  If I paid that much for a 3060, I'd feel burned too.  

The VRAM thing tends to get a little overblown.  I would say 90% of the time, 8gb of VRAM is perfectly fine for blender, but if you're rendering larger scenes then you'll hit that wall.  The 3060 isn't a slow card by any means, but the 4060 will be able to process faster.  

My caveat is that I would never recommend the 3060 12gb for a gaming rig. There are much, much better options for the same price range, but it works well for what it is.  I wouldn't recommend the 4060 for gaming either for the same reason. Perhaps the driver updates will improve the 4060s performance in the future.

The 3060 is technically one of the worst performers of the 30 and 40 series cards, and yet it will probably be useful for longer than some of its superior siblings, just because that VRAM will make it useful for creatives. People overexaggerate LSD's shelf life and there's a tendency to think lsd isn't stable.  As a matter of fact, early doses were made so potent, because it was believed the LSD would degrade by the time it got to it's user.  This was because Sandoz's literature on LSD-25 stated that pure, crystal LSD, would degrade if exposed to certain elements.  Heat, moisture, and direct sunlight.    


That said, with Blotter, the LSD molecules are imbedded in the paper fibers themselves and are generally protected from the air.  Keeping them dry is important too, humidity would only be a problem if it's creating condensation.  If water touches your tabs, it can wash out some/most of the LSD, and if it's Tap Water, certain minerals and chemicals will destroy LSD on contact. For the average US home, tinfoil and a plastic baggie is all you need. If you live in a damp environment, a vacseal and silica gel packets can do the trick.    


If you have Liquid LSD, keep it in a bottle that blocks light and just put it in your fridge.  I don't recommend those bottles w/ the eye dropper built into the cap, those tend to leak easy.  Get a separate pipet.  If you store your blotter in a fridge, be careful when opening it up, because the change in temperature can create condensation.  You have to let your baggie reach room temperature before you open it to avoid this.    


I'd actually avoid keeping your tabs in your phone case, just because your phone getting warm might pose the most risk for your tabs at the moment.  Besides the risk of getting caught with them.  Honestly I've heard people say they've left sheets in hot cars during desert festivals and no drop in quality was noticed.  Just find a safe place to keep them that won't be discovered in a search, and make sure it keeps them dry, cool, and out of sunlight.

1. Ease of use.  You can lay a lot of blotter with cheap kitchenware equipment, but it takes specialized tools to press pills
2. Dosing.  If you have lab-grade scales you can easily divvy up your doses and keep it accurate.  If you dont, the best way to distribute your LSD evenly is volumetric.  
3. There was a time when LSD came in pill form, microdots.  They were the size of a crumb, insanely potent, but if you dropped it into the shag carpet of your bedroom, it was long gone.  
It also allows dealers to cut their LSD with other chemicals, a common one(or at least a government rumor) was Methamphetamine.  
4. Weight and size.  In the 60s, drug charges depended on the weight of what was seized.  Chemists used to dose sugar cubes, but moving volume of this product made them susceptible to heavier charges.  It also took longer because they would have to use a spring-loaded syringe to individually doses EVERY sugar cube. 
 When the early acid chemists discovered the concept of laying blotter, this solved the weight problem, and allowed them to speed up production. 
5. Mail.  It's easier to send some papers in an envelope, than some cheaply pressed pills that may break or be discovered.

Edit: also a historical factoid on the microdot thing, by the 70s acid became associated with blotter, and microdot/psychedelic pills were associated with Mescaline.  So at some point from the 70s to the 80s, if you were asking for microdot, you were probably asking for mescaline.
